title: Getting Help
about: Where to get help, what to save, and who to tell when things go wrong.

cards.prompt:
Scams and online bullying happen to lots of people, including adults and experts. **It's never your fault.** Scammers **count on people feeling embarrassed** and staying quiet, so telling someone is the brave and smart thing to do.

Reports are much easier to act on with **evidence**.

Does each one help, or make things worse?

items.label: Pay a scammer to go away
Delete everything before anyone sees it

cards.explanation: Evidence, a trusted adult and reporting all help. Replying with insults, paying a scammer (they usually ask for more) and deleting the evidence make things worse.
cards.hint: Which ones keep the evidence and get you help? Which ones give a scammer or bully what they want?
cards.nudge: Anything that removes the evidence, or gives a scammer or bully what they want, makes it worse.

cards.prompt:
A **trusted adult** is someone you feel safe talking to: a parent or carer, a teacher, a school counsellor, or an older relative.

If you'd rather talk to someone outside your family, **Kids Helpline** (in Australia) is free, private and open any time, for ages 5 to 25: call **1800 55 1800**. Over 25, or anyone: **Lifeline** on **13 11 14**, any time.

Something online is worrying Ali, and he doesn't want to tell his family yet. What could he do?

options.text: Call Kids Helpline on 1800 55 1800, or talk to a school counsellor
Wait until it's bad enough to be worth telling someone about
options.nudge: You don't need a big problem to ask for help. Look back at who Ali could talk to outside his family.

options.text: Ask people in an online forum, since they can't see who he is
options.nudge: Strangers online aren't trusted adults, and some aren't who they say. Who could Ali talk to that's free and private?

cards.explanation: **Kids Helpline (1800 55 1800)** is free, private and open any time for ages 5 to 25, and a school counsellor is a trusted adult outside the family. Ali doesn't have to wait, or deal with it alone.
cards.hint: The prompt names some people outside the family who can help.

cards.title: Where to report in Australia
cards.body:
Use the app's report button first. Then:

- **eSafety Commissioner** (esafety.gov.au): serious [[cyberbullying]] of anyone under 18 that the app hasn't dealt with, adult cyber abuse, and a **private or nude image** of you shared or threatened (report that straight away).
- **ACCCE**, the Australian Centre to Counter Child Exploitation (accce.gov.au/report): if you're **under 18** and someone pressures or threatens you with a private image. You won't be in trouble.
- **Scamwatch** (scamwatch.gov.au): report a scam, to help warn others.

cards.prompt:
More places to go:

- **Your bank, straight away**, if money or card details are involved.
- **IDCARE** (idcare.org or 1800 595 160): free help to make a plan if your personal details were stolen.
- **ReportCyber** (cyber.gov.au): report cybercrime to the police.
- **In danger right now:** call **000**.

Match each problem to where to go.

pairs.left: A scam you want to warn others about
Someone is in danger right now

cards.explanation: Serious bullying goes to **eSafety** once the app has had a chance; scams to **Scamwatch**; card problems to **your bank** straight away; stolen details to **IDCARE**; and danger right now is always **000**.
cards.hint: Look back at the list on the last card and in this prompt: what is each one for?
cards.nudge: Start with the one you're surest of. What is each service for?

cards.prompt:
**Save the evidence:** before you block someone, screenshot the messages, their username, the web address and the date. Then **block** and **report**.

One exception: if it's a **private or nude image**, **don't copy, save or share the image itself**. Write down the username and where it is, and report it.

In a group chat, some people start posting mean messages about you.

steps.text: It keeps going. What do you do first?

choices.text: Reply with something just as mean
choices.consequence: It usually makes things worse, and it can get you in trouble too.

choices.text: Screenshot the messages, and tell a trusted adult
choices.consequence: You have evidence, and someone on your side.

choices.text: Delete the chat so you don't have to see it
choices.consequence: That deletes the evidence too. Save it first.

choices.text: Report the messages in the app, and block or leave the chat
choices.consequence: The app can remove them. If it doesn't, eSafety can help.
Reporting gives the app, and eSafety if needed, the chance to stop it.

cards.explanation: Don't reply. **Save the evidence**, **tell a trusted adult**, then **report and block**. If the app doesn't act on serious bullying, report it to **eSafety**.
cards.hint: Think about the order: evidence and a trusted adult first, then reporting.

cards.prompt: A scam took money from your card. What's the **first** thing to do?

options.text: Contact the bank straight away (with an adult)
Wait a day to see whether the bank notices and fixes it
options.nudge: Every hour counts with money. Who did the lesson say to contact straight away?

options.text: Post about it online so other people don't get caught too
options.nudge: Warning people is good later. First, stop more money going.

cards.explanation: Contact the **bank straight away**: it may be able to stop the payment or cancel the card. Then report it to **Scamwatch**.
cards.hint: Which place did the lesson say to contact straight away when money is involved?

cards.prompt: Someone you met online says they'll share a private photo of you unless you pay them. If this ever happens: **it is never your fault**, and you won't be in trouble.

steps.text: You feel scared and embarrassed. What do you do?

choices.text: Pay them so it goes away
choices.consequence: Paying usually leads to more demands, not fewer. It's never your fault, and help is there.
You'd lose the evidence and face it alone. It's never your fault, and you don't have to deal with it by yourself.

choices.text: Stop replying, tell a trusted adult, and report it
choices.consequence: You did the right thing. Report it to the app and eSafety (which can help remove images), and if you're under 18, to the ACCCE. Kids Helpline is there any time: 1800 55 1800.

cards.explanation: **It is never your fault**, and you won't be in trouble. **Don't pay** and stop replying. Screenshot the messages and their profile (never the image itself), block them, and **tell a trusted adult**. Report it to the app and to **eSafety** (esafety.gov.au/report). If you're **under 18**, also report it to the **ACCCE** (accce.gov.au/report). Anyone in danger right now: **000**. To talk to someone, any time, for free: **Kids Helpline, 1800 55 1800**.
cards.hint: Look back at where to report a threat about a private image (including for under-18s), and who to tell.

cards.prompt: Late at night, a friend messages you: someone she met online has found out where she lives, and says he's **on his way to her house now**. What should happen first?

options.text: Call 000: she could be in danger right now
Report it to eSafety: it started online
options.nudge: eSafety helps with online abuse, but it can't send help to her door. What's the number for danger right now?

options.text: Screenshot the chat first, then report it
options.nudge: Evidence matters, but not more than her safety. Which number is for someone in danger right now?

cards.explanation: It started online, but someone may be in **danger right now**, so call **000** first. Evidence and reports to the app and eSafety can come later.
cards.hint: Is this about something online, or about someone's safety right now?

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- **Never your fault:** tell an adult, Kids Helpline (1800 55 1800) or Lifeline (13 11 14).
- Report in the app, then eSafety, Scamwatch, your bank or 000.
- **Save evidence** first, but never a private image itself.

That's the course. You know the signs, the steps and where to get help.
